<reason>B landed the debate's sharpest blow—the "hostage baby" dilemma that turned A's proposed enforcement mechanism against A's own opening—and pressed a coherent "certificate is a brochure / legitimation expands demand" thesis to the end. But A absorbed the hit honestly (A1: baby gets recognition; sanction runs through parental liability, agency prosecution, and a slow versus fast lane), then converted B's own materials: B's "refuse the operator a licence" collapses toward the motion, B's adoption analogy admits prohibition, and above all B's week-twenty timing point indicts B's purely ex-post liability regime. A's closing made the decisive weighing clean—conditions of entry arrive before conception, liability arrives after the harm—while B never squarely rebutted A1.4's relocation argument, left its own regime (prohibition-lite with surrogate immunity) somewhat murky, and rested its final weighing on an asserted rather than argued claim that state licensing swells demand into uncertified clinics. B also clipped every speech, a recurring execution cost. Competitive, but A gave the third-party reader the cleaner reason to vote on the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.1–B2.3: "The child is the leverage" exposed that A's recognition-conditioning enforcement would manufacture the stranded infant A opened with, forcing A to retreat to friction-based deterrence—though A's A5.3 turnaround of B's own week-twenty timing point against ex-post liability was the cleanest counterstrike.</best_rebuttal>
